lesson.title: Why Bigger Samples Feel Steadier: The Standard Deviation of x-bar
lesson.summary: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x-bar equals the population standard deviation sigma divided by the square root of n, showing that averaging more observations produces less variable estimates.
lesson.body:
Knowing that x-bar is centered on mu says nothing about how far a typical sample mean might land from that center. The standard deviation of x-bar answers that question, and just like with the sample proportion, it depends heavily on the sample size.

The formula can be derived using the same random variable rules used for the sample proportion. Think of a sample as n independent observations, X1 through Xn, each drawn from a population with standard deviation sigma. From the rules for combining independent random variables, the variance of a sum of independent random variables equals the sum of their variances, so the variance of X1 + X2 + ... + Xn equals n times sigma squared. Since x-bar equals that sum divided by n, and dividing a random variable by a constant divides its variance by the square of that constant, the variance of x-bar equals (n)(sigma squared) divided by n squared, which simplifies to sigma squared divided by n. Taking the square root gives the standard deviation of x-bar: sigma divided by the square root of n.

Here is a worked example. Suppose annual salaries at a large company have a population standard deviation of sigma = 12 thousand dollars, and a sample of n = 36 employees is drawn. The standard deviation of x-bar is 12 divided by the square root of 36, which is 12 divided by 6, which equals 2. So sample means from repeated samples of 36 employees would typically differ from the true population mean by about 2 thousand dollars, noticeably tighter than the 12 thousand dollar spread of individual salaries.

That comparison is the heart of why this formula matters: individual observations vary by sigma, but averages of n observations vary by only sigma divided by the square root of n, which shrinks as n grows. This is why polls and studies with larger samples produce more reliable estimates, and why quadrupling a sample size only cuts the standard deviation in half rather than to a quarter, since the square root of 4 is 2, not 4. As with the sample proportion, this formula assumes observations are effectively independent, which is reasonable when sampling with replacement, or when sampling without replacement from a population that is large relative to the sample, the same 10 percent condition introduced earlier in this unit for the sample proportion.
